Learning Objectives
Define and describe the classification of congenital scoliosis.
Assess the natural history of congenital scoliosis.
Define the treatment objectives for congenital scoliosis and the indications for surgery.
Describe the new classification of early-onset scoliosis.
Define the treatment objectives and surgical indications for idiopathic early-onset scoliosis.
Congenital Scoliosis
Definition
Deformity from vertebral anomalies in utero




NOTES
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
1/29

Develops during the first 6 weeks of intrauterine life
Congenital scoliosis is a deformity of the spine from vertebral anomalies that develop during
the first 5 to 8 weeks of intrauterine life, at which time the mesenchymal tissue forms the
anatomic scaffold of the spine.1,2
Prevalence and Etiology
The cause of congenital scoliosis is unknown.
Associated with hypoxia,3,4 carbon monoxide exposure,5,6 valproic acid,7 boric acid,8 fetal
alcohol syndrome,9 and hyperthermia10
Pathoanatomy
Failure of formation
Wedge vertebra
Hemivertebra
Failure of segmentation
Block vertebra
Unilateral bar
Mixed failure of formation and failure of segmentation

Pathoanatomy
Congenital scoliosis is an abnormal development of the spine.2 It is further categorized
as a failure of formation (Figure 1), failure of segmentation (Figure 2), or a mix of both.
Failure of formation is evidenced by an abnormally shaped bone/vertebrae. The mildest
form is a wedged vertebra composed of two pedicles and a trapezoid-shaped vertebra.
Four types of hemivertebrae also are associated with failure of formation. A fully
segmented hemivertebra has a disk space above and below, a partially hemivertebra is
fused to an adjacent vertebra on one side and a disk on the other side, and an
unsegmented hemivertebra is fused to the levels above and below. An incarcerated
hemivertebra, which is ovoid and smaller than a fully segmented hemivertebra, causes
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
2/29

minimal scoliosis because the vertebrae above and below compensate for the deformity.
In general, the more distinct and separate the end plates of each hemivertebra, the
greater the progression of scoliosis over time.
Failure of segmentation is evidenced by a bony bar. A block vertebra is a congenitally
malformed vertebra that is fused to the segment above or below. Conversely, a
unilateral segmentation (bar) defect is caused by a bony tether on only one side of the
vertebra, causing restricted growth on the affected side.
Figure 1 Illustrations show spine formation defects. A, Wedge vertebra. B, Fully
segmented hemivertebra. C, Partially segmented hemivertebra. D, Unsegmented
hemivertebra. (Reproduced from Hedequist D, Emans J: Congenital scoliosis. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2004;12[4]:266-275.)
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
3/29

Figure 2 Illustrations show spine segmentation defects. A, Block vertebra. B, Unilateral
segmentation (bar) defect. C, Unilateral segmentation (bar) defect with a contralateral
hemivertebra. (Reproduced from Hedequist D, Emans J: Congenital scoliosis. J Am Acad
Orthop Surg 2004;12[4]:266-275.)
Natural History
Depends on the vertebral anomaly and remaining growth.2
A unilateral segmentation (bar) defect with a contralateral hemivertebra(e) is the most
progressive form of congenital scoliosis.
Two periods of accelerated growth: first 2 years of life and the adolescent growth spurt
A T1 through T12 thoracic height of less than18 cm leads to poor pulmonary function as an
adult.11

Natural History
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
4/29

The natural history and risk of progression of congenital scoliosis depend on the
vertebral anomaly and the growth remaining for the patient. The chart shown in Figure
3 illustrates the manner in which the type of vertebral anomaly affects the rate of
scoliosis progression. A unilateral segmentation (bar) defect with contralateral
hemivertebra(e) is associated with the poorest prognosis. Regarding growth potential,
children typically undergo two periods of accelerated development: one during the first 2
years of life and another during adolescence.
Figure 3 Chart shows the median yearly rate of deterioration (in degrees) without
management for each type of single congenital scoliosis in each region of the spine (187
patients). The numbers on the lower end of the range in each column refer to patients
who were seen before age 10 years; the numbers on the upper end of the range in each
column refer to patients who were seen at or older than age 10 years. (Adapted with
permission from McMaster MJ, Ohtsuka K: The natural history of congenital scoliosis: A
study of two hundred and fifty-one patients. J Bone Joint Surg Am 1982;64[8]:1128-1147.)
During management of congenital scoliosis, the effects of arresting spinal growth in any
portion of the thoracic spine must be considered. Karol et al11 showed that patients who
undergo early spinal fusion (ie, with <18 cm of T1 through T12 thoracic height at
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
5/29

maturity) were more likely to have poorer pulmonary function compared with patients
with longer thoracic height (Figure 4).
Figure 4 Graph shows thoracic height (ht) at the time of follow-up compared with the
percentage of predicted forced vital capacity (FVC). Patients with the shortest thoracic
spine height (measured from T1 to T12) had the greatest restriction of pulmonary
volume (r = 0.73, P < 0.001). (Reproduced with permission from Karol LA, Johnston C,
Mladenov K, Schochet P, Walters P, Browne RH: Pulmonary function following early
thoracic fusion in non-neuromuscular scoliosis. J Bone Joint Surg Am 2008;90[6]:1272-
1281.)
Associated Conditions
Spinal cord malformation (occurs in as many as 37% of patients with congenital scoliosis)1,12-15
Cardiac anomalies15
Renal anomalies1,15
Other anomalies

Associated Conditions
Congenital scoliosis is associated with several other conditions. In studies of patients
with congenital scoliosis, as many as 37% had an associated abnormality observed on
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
6/29

MRI of the spine, including syringomyelia, Arnold-Chiari malformation, and
diastematomyelia. Congenital cardiac abnormalities were found in 26% of patients, with
33% of affected individuals requiring surgical treatment for these cardiac issues.
Therefore, an echocardiogram is recommended in patients with congenital scoliosis,
especially in those undergoing surgical treatment. Another commonly associated
condition is urogenital defects, which affect 21% to 34% of patients with congenital
scoliosis, depending on the series. Screening via renal ultrasonography or MRI is
recommended in this patient population, especially if surgical treatment is planned.
Other concurrent abnormalities include Klippel-Feil syndrome, cranial nerve palsy, radial
hypoplasia, clubfeet, dislocated hips, Sprengel deformity, imperforate anus, hemifacial
macrosomia, and VATER/VACTERL. VACTERL is an acronym for a constellation of birth
defects: V = vertebral anomalies, A = anal atresia, C = cardiac defects, T = tracheal
anomalies, E = esophageal atresia, R = renal abnormalities, and L = other limb
abnormalities.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Imaging Studies
Early supine radiograph16,17
Initial upright PA/lateral radiographs of the entire spine as baseline to evaluate curve
progression
CT with three-dimensional reconstruction images to evaluate bony anatomy
MRI to evaluate for associated intraspinal abnormalities14,15,18
Cardiac echocardiogram/renal ultrasonography/MRI1,15

Imaging Studies
In congenital scoliosis, an early supine radiographic series is scheduled to evaluate the
vertebral anomaly, whereas initial upright radiographs (AP and lateral) serve as the
baseline for evaluating curve progression; the entire spine, including the cervical spine,
should be imaged. Cobb measurements often are less accurate because of the abnormal
anatomy; therefore, progression should be assessed by comparing current radiographs
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
7/29

with previous radiographs. CT with three-dimensional reconstruction images may be
helpful in preoperative planning. Because of possible associated intraspinal
abnormalities, MRI also is recommended, especially as part of the preoperative
evaluation and/or with abnormal neurologic findings. For evaluation of associated
congenital abnormalities, cardiac echocardiography and renal ultrasonography or MRI
may be warranted preoperatively.
Physical Examination
Assess for patient asymmetry and balance (ie, sagittal and coronal planes).
Other findings

Physical Examination
In patients with congenital scoliosis, existing balance and alignment (ie, in the coronal
and sagittal planes) should be evaluated. Shoulder and pelvic alignment and deviation of
the head/trunk from the center of the pelvis should be documented. In addition, a
comprehensive neurologic examination will establish a baseline for discerning future
decline and/or changes. Limb-length inequalities also should be evaluated to determine
if they contribute to apparent but nonstructural scoliosis.
In addition to evaluating balance and alignment of the spine, physical examination of
patients with congenital scoliosis should include inspection for midline abnormalities,
such as dimples, hairy patches, or other sinus tracts. Range of motion of the cervical
spine, thoracic spine, and lumbar spine and the scapular position and mobility should be
noted. Finally, abnormalities of the feet (eg, cavus feet) should be documented because
they may indicate an intraspinal abnormality, such as a tethered cord or intraspinal
tumor.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
8/29

Observation if congenital scoliosis is nonprogressive13,17,19-22
Cast immobilization; less successful with congenital scoliosis than with idiopathic scoliosis but
may be used for compensatory curvature or to delay surgical management

Nonsurgical Management
A congenital spine abnormality requires observation, especially during periods of rapid
growth, to monitor progression. Depending on the type of congenital scoliosis,
observation alone may be sufficient if the deformity is not progressing. Cast or brace
immobilization is indicated only as a temporary measure to control compensatory
curves while allowing for continued spinal growth or to delay surgical treatment until a
child is older.23
Surgical Management
Performed before development of a major deformity
The goal is to achieve a balanced spine while maintaining flexibility and preserving normal
growth.
May be associated with a higher risk for neurologic complications than other pediatric spinal
procedures.18

Surgical Management
The goal of surgical management of congenital scoliosis is to maintain a balanced spine
while preserving growth and flexibility. Surgical management often is performed before
a major deformity develops or large compensatory curves become structural. The risk of
neurologic complications may be higher in this subset of patients than in those
undergoing other pediatric spine procedures because of the abnormal anatomy and the
younger age at surgical treatment.
Techniques

Convex hemiepiphysiodesis (Figure 5)
Requires substantial overall growth and concave growth potential
Anterior procedure
Removal of convex disk and end plates
Fusion of the convex portion with a bone graft
Posterior procedure
Unilateral removal of the facet joint and fusion
Instrumentation with the use of pedicle screws, wires, or hooks
Immobilization for 3 to 6 months until fusion is complete

Hemivertebra excision (Figures 6 and 7)

of the spine of a 4-year-old child who underwent hemivertebra excision. (Courtesy of Selina Poon,

Figure 7 Images of the spine of a boy with congenital scoliosis. A, PA radiograph demonstrates
congenital left thoracic scoliosis because of a left T6 fully segmented hemivertebra (arrow) with a
contralateral unsegmented bar between T5 and T7. Intraoperative photographs show anterior
convex hemiepiphysiodesis, including convex disk excision (B) and the use of a rib strut graft (C),
followed by placement of a concave growing rod to control the remaining spine. D, PA radiograph
obtained 4 years postoperatively demonstrates a stable spine. The patient’s scoliosis was well
maintained via consecutive rod lengthening. (Reproduced with permission from Tsirikos AI:
Congenital deformities of the spine, in Yazici M, ed: Non-Idiopathic Spine Deformities in Young
Children. Berlin, Germany, Springer, 2011, pp 45-72.)
Distraction-based growing rod (Figure 8)
Used to control deformity and delay final fusion in patients with multiple congenital spinal
deformities and inadequate thoracic length
Depending on the type of implant, lengthening is repeated every 1 to 6 months (ie,
outpatient surgery or office-based procedures)
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
13/29

Figure 8 Preoperative AP radiograph (A) and three-dimensional CT reconstruction image (B) and
postoperative AP (C) and lateral (D) radiographs of the spine of a 13-year-old patient with
hemivertebra at T2, T5, and T11 who underwent hemivertebra excision and long fusion.
(Courtesy of Selina Poon, MD, Tampa, FL.)
Anterior and posterior fusion with or without instrumentation
Used for immature individuals who are not appropriate candidates for hemivertebrectomy
but have adequate thoracic length
Decreases risk for crankshaft phenomenon and pseudarthrosis
Posterior spinal fusion with or without instrumentation
Used in older children with adequate thoracic height who are unlikely to experience the
crankshaft phenomenon
Postoperative immobilization is important if the procedure is not instrumented.

Techniques
Convex hemiepiphysiodesis slows growth on the convex side of the deformity while
allowing for continued growth of the concave side. For this technique to be successful,
the patient must have enough growth potential for deformity correction (ie, usually <6
years). The anterior procedure involves the removal of the convex disk and end plate
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
14/29

and fusion of the convex portion of the deformity. In most children, the anterior portion
of the procedure may be performed via a posterior approach with appropriate planning
and retraction of the neural elements. Conversely, the posterior portion of the
procedure requires unilateral removal of the facet joints and arthrodesis. Pedicle screws
or a hook construct may provide increased support for convex-sided fusion. The patient
is then immobilized for 3 to 6 months in a cast/brace until fusion is achieved. To ensure
that growth is slowed only on the convex side, the concave side must not be exposed (ie,
to minimize the risk of fusion).
Hemivertebra excision is indicated in patients with a progressive deformity and a trunk
imbalance caused by the hemivertebra. It may be performed via a combined anterior
and posterior procedure or via a posterior approach alone. With hemivertebra excision,
the best results tend to occur in patients younger than 6 years with flexible curvatures of
less than 40°. For ease of implant placement and soft-tissue coverage, this procedure is
ideally performed after patients reach age 2.5 years.
In patients with congenital scoliosis, distraction-based growing constructs may be
attached to the spine or ribs to control the deformity and delay final fusion. This
technique may be useful in skeletally immature patients with a progressive deformity
and multiple discrete congenital abnormalities of the spine but who are not appropriate
candidates for spinal fusion because of inadequate thoracic length; however,
lengthening must be repeated every 1 to 6 months for continued spinal growth.
Depending on the type of implants used, lengthening may be performed as an
outpatient surgical procedure or in the office.
Some children with congenital scoliosis have large progressive curves with multiple
congenitally malformed spinal elements rather than a focal hemivertebra. If these
children are skeletally immature but have adequate thoracic length, the risk of
crankshaft deformity with posterior only fusion is high. An anterior and posterior fusion
procedure can be performed in this situation. The crankshaft phenomenon is defined as
a progressive rotational and angular spinal deformity that occurs after posterior spine
surgery; it is thought to occur secondary to continued growth of the anterior elements of
the spine after solid posterior fusion, resulting in a twisting of the spine to accommodate
this anterior growth. An anterior and posterior fusion procedure decreases the risks for
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
15/29

the crankshaft phenomenon and pseudarthrosis compared with a posterior only
technique; however, this procedure may be associated with more surgical morbidity
than posterior only procedures because a thoracotomy or retroperitoneal approach is
necessary. The addition of instrumentation may improve fusion rates and correction but
is associated with a higher risk of iatrogenic injury secondary to abnormal anatomy.
The posterior spinal fusion technique is limited to older children who are close to
skeletal maturity because of the potential risk for the crankshaft phenomenon caused by
uncontrolled anterior spinal growth.24 Instrumentation adds stability to the fusion and
decreases the risk of pseudarthrosis; however, it may increase the risk of iatrogenic
neurologic injury secondary to abnormal anatomy.
Early-Onset Scoliosis
Definition
Early-onset scoliosis (EOS) is defined as a spinal deformity with onset before age 10 years.
Often associated with thoracic insufficiency syndrome

Definition
EOS is defined as any spinal deformity with onset before age 10 years. The condition
encompasses a heterogeneous group of diagnoses based on the etiology of the
deformity,25,26 including idiopathic, syndromic, neuromuscular, and congenital scoliosis
(Resource 1). Because spinal growth often is coupled with growth of the thorax and
lungs, EOS frequently is associated with thoracic insufficiency syndrome, or the inability
of the thorax to support normal respiration and lung growth.
Respiratory Function
The goal of EOS management is to preserve respiratory function.27-29
Normal lungs continue to develop until age 8 years.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
16/29

Respiratory failure in patients with EOS occurs secondary to intrinsic and extrinsic factors.

Respiratory Function
In normal lung, development of the alveoli is complete by age 2 years, with airway
enlargement continuing until age 5 years and alveolar hyperplasia continuing until age 8
years.
In children with unmanaged EOS, respiratory failure is well documented and contributes
to higher mortality rates compared with rates in the general population. Respiratory
failure is caused by intrinsic (ie, failure of alveolar multiplication) and extrinsic (ie, rib and
chest wall deformities) factors. In EOS, intrinsic failure because of chest deformity
prevents hyperplasia and development of the lung tissue, whereas the extrinsic rib and
chest wall deformity leads to loss of compliance or functional incompetence of the chest
wall. Because of the risk of thoracic insufficiency syndrome, management of EOS focuses
on maintaining growth of the thorax and lung volume.
Classification of EOS

Classification of EOS
Because the patient population with congenital EOS is heterogeneous, comparison of
treatment options and outcomes has been almost impossible. However, a new
classification system, known as C-EOS, has been created to describe and categorize EOS,
considering patient age, etiology, Cobb angle of the major curve, sagittal kyphosis, and
the annual progression ratio30 (Figure 9; Resource 2).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
17/29

Figure 9 Chart shows the classification of early-onset scoliosis. This classification system
consists of a continuous prefix (age), three core variables (etiology, major curve angle,
and kyphosis), and an optional modifier (curve progression). APR = annual progression
ratio; (-), N, and (+) are kyphosis variables; P = progression modifier. (Adapted with
permission from Williams BA, Matsumoto H, McCalla DJ, et al: Development and initial
validation of the Classification of Early-Onset Scoliosis (C-EOS). J Bone Joint Surg Am
2014;96[16]:1359-1367.)
Infantile Idiopathic EOS
Infantile idiopathic EOS is diagnosed in patients younger than 4 years.28,31-38
No known cause
More than 90% of cases resolve without management.
May spontaneously resolve if the rib-vertebral angle difference (RVAD) is less than 20° and/or
a phase 1 rib is observed on radiographs
MRI should be considered for curvatures greater than 20°.

Infantile Idiopathic EOS
Infantile idiopathic EOS is diagnosed in patients younger than 4 years. The cause of the
deformity is unknown, but more than 90% of cases resolve without management. Signs
of progression are a RVAD greater than 20° and/or a phase 2 rib at the apex of the curve.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
18/29

The RVAD is determined by the intersection of a line perpendicular to the apical vertebra
end plate with a line from the mid-neck to the mid-head of the corresponding rib. The
RVAD is the difference between the angle of a line drawn perpendicular to the end plate
of the apical thoracic vertebrae and a line drawn down the middle of the concave and
convex ribs. The RVAD is calculated by subtracting the measurement of the concave
angle from the measurement of the convex angle. If the RVAD is less than 20°, idiopathic
EOS may spontaneously resolve and, therefore, requires only continued observation
(Figure 10).
Figure 10 Illustration shows measurement of the rib-vertebra angle difference in
patients with idiopathic scoliosis. A line is drawn perpendicular to the end plate of the
apical vertebra (a). A second line is drawn from the midpoint of the neck of the rib at the
apical vertebra through the midpoint of the head of the same rib and extending to the
perpendicular on the convex side (b). The angle between these two lines is calculated.
The angle on the concave side is calculated in a similar manner. The rib-vertebra angle
difference is calculated by subtracting the angle on the convex side from the angle on
the concave side of the curve. (Adapted with permission from Mehta MH: The rib-
vertebra angle in the early diagnosis between resolving and progressive infantile
scoliosis. J Bone Joint Surg Br 1972;54[2]:230-243.)
Another indication of spontaneous resolution is the phase of the rib head at the apex of
the curve. For patients with a phase 1 rib, no overlap of the rib head with the apical
vertebral body is present. If overlap of the rib head with the apical vertebral body is
present, a phase 2 rib classification is assigned, and resolution is less likely33,36 (Figure
11; Resource 3).
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
19/29

Conversely, curvatures diagnosed after age year and larger curves at diagnosis are
associated with an increased risk of progression. Plagiocephaly, developmental dysplasia
of the hip, inguinal hernia, and congenital heart disease often are associated with this
condition. In addition, the reported incidence of neural axis abnormalities has been
reported to be as high as 21% (range, 13% to 21%). Therefore, MRI evaluation should be
considered, while also weighing the potential risks of sedation in this age group.
Figure 11 Illustrations show rib-vertebra relationships in patients with idiopathic
scoliosis. A, Phase 1 rib-vertebra relationship: no overlap of the rib head and the
vertebral body. B, Phase 2 rib-vertebra relationship: overlap of the rib head on the
vertebral body indicates curve progression. (Adapted with permission from Mehta MH:
The rib-vertebra angle in the early diagnosis between resolving and progressive infantile
scoliosis. J Bone Joint Surg Br 1972;54[2]:230-243.)
Juvenile Idiopathic Scoliosis
Diagnosed between age 4 and 10 years28,34,39-43 (Resources 4 and 5)
Older children—The condition resembles adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, with a predominance
of right-sided curves and more girls affected than boys.
Curvatures are more likely to progress to require surgical management.
Neural axis abnormalities in 18% to 26% of cases; therefore, MRI should be considered
Currently, vertebral body tethering is a novel treatment option for juvenile idiopathic scoliosis.
Congenital disorder
Deformity because of vertebral anomalies in utero
Develops during the first 6 weeks of intrauterine life
Neuromuscular and syndromic EOS
Neuromuscular scoliosis occurs in children with an underlying medical condition that affects
their neurologic/muscular system.
Syndromic scoliosis occurs as part of a genetic or nongenetic syndrome.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
20/29

In neuromuscular and syndromic scoliosis, the natural history of the underlying condition
dictates the risk of progression and the appropriate treatment option and strategies.
Surgical risks are associated with poor nutrition, respiratory issues, the soft-tissue envelope,
and decreased bone density.

Juvenile Idiopathic Scoliosis
Juvenile idiopathic scoliosis is diagnosed in patients aged 4 to 10 years. Dissimilar from
patients with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, patients with juvenile idiopathic scoliosis
often require continued monitoring and surgical treatment because of their age at
diagnosis. Similar to the infantile form of idiopathic EOS, the incidence of concurrent
neural axis abnormalities ranges from 18% to 26%; therefore, MRI evaluation is
recommended. A new treatment option known as vertebral body tethering may be
considered in this group of patients.
Neuromuscular scoliosis, which occurs as part of a patient’s underlying medical
condition, affects the neurologic or muscular system. Syndromic scoliosis occurs as part
of a syndrome. The risk of a spinal curve corresponds with the severity of a child’s
condition. The risks and complications of management also are related to the severity of
the underlying disease and may include increased rates of infection, wound
complications, implant loosening, implant failure, and even death.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Cast immoblization23,36,44,45
May be effective in resolving idiopathic curves if initiated before age 2 years
Applied under anesthesia in traction, derotated and flexed away from the concavity of the
curve
Changed every 8 to 12 weeks
In curves that resolve or are stabilized, bracing may help maintain correction through
skeletal maturity.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:46 AM
AAOS | Congenital Scoliosis and Early-Onset Scoliosis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001176
21/29

In nonidiopathic curves, used to delay surgical management

Nonsurgical Management
Serial cast immobilization is used to manage EOS. In patients with curves less than 60°
who undergo cast immobilization before age 19 months, curvature is reduced to less
than 10° at maturity. Serial casts are applied under general anesthesia and are changed
every 8 to 12 weeks. Traction, derotation, and flexion force typically is used to correct the
deformity. In curves that have stabilized, a brace is used to maintain the correction. For
larger and non-idiopathic curvatures, cast immobilization has been used to delay
surgical management.
If EOS can no longer be controlled via nonsurgical management, then surgical
management is required to maintain a balanced spine while preserving growth and
flexibility (Resource 6).
Surgical Management
Techniques
Early fusion11,46-48
Prevents future spinal growth
Results in restrictive lung disease because of limited intrathoracic and lung volume
Used only if a limited number of vertebrae are fused (ie, hemivertebra)
Early fusion is reserved for short-segment deformities that are progressive secondary to the
effects on lung growth and development.

Techniques
If cast and brace immobilization can no longer control an EOS deformity or are not
tolerated, several types of distraction-based implants may be used: a vertically
expandable prosthetic titanium rib, dual submuscular rods, and magnetic controlled
growing rods. Anchors may be placed on the ribs or spine to control the deformity and
delay final fusion; however, lengthening must be repeated every 2 to 6 months for
continued spinal growth. Depending on the type of implant used, this procedure may be
performed as an outpatient surgical procedure or in the office. To enhance the
correction of a chest wall deformity, lengthening may be combined with an expansion
thoracoplasty; however, the law of diminishing returns applies here. Subsequent gains in
spine lengthening tend to decrease over time while force requirements increase.
Vertebral body tethering is a novel technique that involves growth modulation to correct
spinal deformity without fusion; however, complication rates with this method may be as
high as 41%. Although the indications for vertebral body tethering currently are under
investigation, the technique holds promise for the management of juvenile idiopathic
scoliosis.

Complications are a common, seemingly inevitable consequence of the surgical
management of EOS because progressive deformity starts at such a young age in these
patients. If a patient with EOS has associated medical conditions, the risk of
complications is even higher. Because the goal of surgical management of EOS is to
promote continued growth of the immature chest wall and spine, many of the treatment
options discussed require multiple, recurring interventions with repeated use of
anesthesia and hospitalizations. Therefore, these patients have an increased risk for
infection and wound dehiscence, especially if the same incision is used for multiple
surgical procedures. If patients also have impaired nutritional status secondary to other
medical problems, the risks are even higher. To minimize wound complications, skin
flaps should be developed for full-thickness coverage, and skin closure should be under
minimal tension. In addition, postoperative padding may be used to minimize pressure
on the skin.
Implant-related complications also are common in patients with EOS because of their
relatively small size and the continued growth of the spine. Rod fracture, anchor failure,
anchor migration, and prominent hardware are frequently encountered by surgeons
who manage EOS.
